implementation_notes: queue.Queue is the standard-library point-to-point channel for threads: get() removes exactly one item and blocks until one is available, put() blocks when maxsize is reached, and the documented worker pattern calls task_done() so join() can drain the queue. Work is distributed to whichever worker calls get() first, which is exactly the one-consumer contract with fan-out; multiprocessing.Queue extends the same contract across processes, and a broker (RabbitMQ, Redis) is required only for durability or cross-host channels.
code_sketch:
import queue, threading
q = queue.Queue(maxsize=100)
for _ in range(4):
    threading.Thread(
        target=lambda: [handle(j) for j in iter(q.get, None)], daemon=True).start()
q.put(job)          # exactly one worker gets this job
pitfalls: get() with block=True and no timeout can wait uninterruptibly (documented platform caveat); shutdown needs a sentinel or a timeout loop, since Queue.shutdown() only exists from 3.13.
Queue is not reentrant and asyncio queues are not thread-safe - mixing the two in one design breaks the contract silently.
A worker that calls get() but never task_done() makes join() hang forever.

variants.name: asyncio.Queue with worker coroutines
variants.implementation_notes: asyncio.Queue provides the same FIFO put/get contract for coroutines: get() awaits instead of blocking a thread, and the documentation's example distributes workload across several concurrent worker tasks that call task_done() so join() can drain. Choose it for a single-threaded async service; use queue.Queue or multiprocessing.Queue when the work is blocking or CPU-bound, because a blocking call inside a worker coroutine stalls the whole event loop.
variants.code_sketch:
import asyncio
async def main():
    q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)
    for _ in range(4):
        asyncio.create_task(worker(q))     # competitors on one queue
    for j in batch: await q.put(j)
    await q.join()                         # drain until task_done() balances puts
pitfalls: asyncio.Queue is not thread-safe; a producer thread must marshal through loop.call_soon_threadsafe or the loop corrupts state.
QueueShutDown exists only from 3.13 - older runtimes stop workers with sentinel values, which must be put per worker or the last ones hang.
Awaiting work inside the consumer loop serializes it; parallel consumption needs several worker tasks, and task_done() accounting must then still match every put().
